Patch Set 1:

AI code review results below, please doublecheck

Some concerns, see inline comments.

The bigger question is whether this should be a patch at all. The three commits it documents and tests ("lfs: find --since", "lfs: find --changelog", "lfs: find --since-cookie") each add a user-visible option with no man page entry and no test case, and this one lands all of them afterwards. Earlier commits in the same series shipped their man pages and tests with the code (llapi_scan_changelog.3 and llapi_scan_changelog_test.c, lfind.8), so folding each of these three hunks back into the commit it describes would keep that pattern and let the documentation be reviewed against the implementation it belongs to.

Uploaded patch set 2.

commit.subject: LU-20650 tests: sanity cases for find's changelog flags
commit.message:
LU-20650 tests: sanity cases for find's changelog flags

lfs-find.1 gains --since, --since-cookie, --changelog and --resolve:
what each answers, that --since is a strict subset of the same search
without it, that a bare index belongs to one MDT and is refused where
that is ambiguous, that a number which could be an index or an epoch
second is never guessed at, and that reading a changelog neither
consumes it nor needs a registered user while records exist only while
some user is registered.

Four sanity cases.  160aa asserts the promise --since is worth having
-- that its answer is a subset of the same find without it, and a
smaller one -- rather than asserting a particular file, so it does not
depend on what else the filesystem is doing.  160ab walks the
refusals: -size, an object time, --maxdepth, a path below the mount
and an unknown MDT are each refused, and --resolve lets the first of
them through.  160ac runs the cookie three times: the first writes it,
the second returns the new object and not the old one, the third
returns nothing, and then a stale anchor and both anchors together are
refused.  160ad hardlinks one file into two directories and searches
under each of them.

160ac asks for creations only.  A wide mask records the test's own
reads, and then "nothing changed since" is never true -- which is what
hid an off-by-one in the cookie until a narrow mask made every run
repeat the last object of the one before it.

A test that asserts a precondition instead of creating one only holds
where that precondition happens to be true.  160ac's stale anchor is
made rather than assumed -- records the cookie has not consumed, then
a purge, then one more past the hole -- because writing index 1 is
only older than the oldest surviving record on a filesystem that
already has changelog history.  On a fresh one index 1 IS the oldest
record, nothing was purged, and refusing would be wrong.

160ac also feeds the cookie two files it is never written with: one
whose MDT index is negative, and one whose header names another
filesystem.  Neither is a bad anchor to ignore -- the first indexes
the anchor array far past its end, and the second is a whole-log
rescan of this filesystem plus the loss of the other one's anchors --
so one has to be ignored and the other refused, and the file it
refuses has to still be there afterwards.

160aa names the files it expects rather than only counting them, since
a count that merely shrank is also satisfied by returning nothing, and
it widens the gap around its window so a node that spends seconds in
sync does not change what the test means.

160ab's --resolve case asserts that the option is accepted and
deliberately does not assert the answer.  Resolution does not yet fill
the size -- every object comes back "could not be decided", even one
with bytes in it -- so asserting a match there would encode as correct
what the man page promises and the code does not yet do.

The tag is tests: rather than doc: because that is where the bulk of
the change is; the man page rides along because the options it
describes are the ones these cases exercise.

The gate is CLIENT_VERSION.  Nothing in this series touches server
code -- it is lustreapi.h, lustre/utils/ and Documentation/ -- so the
options work against any server old enough to have changelogs, and
gating on the MDS skipped interop runs that would have passed while
leaving an old client unguarded.

160ab also covers the two things that make --changelog worth having
over --since, which the man page leads with and nothing exercised: an
object unlinked since its event is still in the answer, and its FID
names it once no pathname does.  Writing that case is what found the
second half missing -- find_decide() counted the object as having no
pathname instead of printing its FID, so the one thing --since cannot
report came back silently absent.

160ab also covers what a record cannot answer and now says so: -perm
and -links join the refusals, -name is exercised because a record
whose events are all data stores carries no name and that used to
reach fnmatch() with NULL, --resolve on its own is refused rather than
dropped, and a subtree search under --resolve has to answer for that
subtree and not the whole filesystem.

A changelog names an object by FID, and fid2path answers with one of
its names -- the first linkea entry, the one the file was created
under.  So a search rooted at the other directory is answered about a
name that is not under it, and -name is answered about a basename the
object also does not go by there.  160ad is the case for that: without
the links being walked it finds the file under a and loses it under b,
which is a silent miss and the worst shape a wrong answer can take.
